Executive Summary
Market Updates

blocks.html: Over the last quarter, the global macroeconomic and aviation landscape continued to evolve, with year-end publication of 2026 industry outlooks informing the key takeaways. Below we have summarized where we believe the aviation industry stands as of Q4 2025.
blocks.text: Over the last quarter, the global macroeconomic and aviation landscape continued to evolve, with year-end publication of 2026 industry outlooks informing the key takeaways. Below we have summarized where we believe the aviation industry stands as of Q4 2025.

items: Demand & Traffic Growth: Global air traffic growth remains structurally strong, with passenger origin-destination traffic projected to double by 2045, driven primarily by Asia-Pacific demand, where rising incomes and air travel penetration are expected to account for nearly half of global traffic over the long term

Fleet Growth & Supply Constraints: The global passenger fleet is projected to grow from approximately 30,800 aircraft today to ~51,900 by 2045, requiring nearly 48,000 new aircraft deliveries, over half of which are replacement-driven.1 Near-term OEM delivery bottlenecks—particularly related to engines and MRO capacity—are expected to persist through the latter part of the decade, supporting elevated lease rates and asset utilization for in-service aircraft.

Financing & Leasing Environment: While funding costs remain elevated relative to recent historical levels, airlines’ continued demand for leased aircraft, together with durable lease structures and disciplined lessor supply, supports attractive risk-adjusted returns for aircraft owners.

blocks.text: Aircraft Fund & Business Update

items: As of December 2025, the Fund has completed multiple successful closings, ending the year with over $300M of capital commitments and we expect to complete additional closes during the Q1 2026. While the fundraising period is set to expire at the end of Q1 2026, we are considering an extension to allow prospective investors more time to complete their due diligence.

During Q4 2025, the Griffin platform successfully completed its inaugural master trust securitization, representing the largest-ever aircraft ABS transaction. The $1.2Bn issuance was backed by a diversified portfolio of Griffin’s existing young, new-technology commercial aircraft on long-term leases to high-quality airline counterparties.

In addition to a mix of existing Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 aircraft, the issuance was also backed by a diversified pool of 9x aircraft on lease to 8x lessees that were acquired in tandem with the securitization during the quarter. These aircraft were integral to the securitization, supporting portfolio diversification efforts and helping facilitate our success in realizing the attractive terms achieved. Importantly, the Aircraft Fund holds an ~ 19% equity interest in this 9x aircraft pool, directly participating in the economics of the securitized assets and benefiting from the improved liquidity and financing efficiency associated with the ABS structure.

Over the course of the quarter, we worked to begin the closing process for our new aircraft acquisitions and begin transferring existing assets from the Griffin Corporate Entity to the ABS structure. As we enter 2026, we are continuing to finalize the closing and integration of the remaining new aircraft associated with this portfolio, further reinforcing the Aircraft Fund’s exposure to scaled, institutional-quality financing and liquidity generation across the Griffin platform.

We are actively evaluating several potential investments for the Fund and are excited for the year ahead as we continue to grow the portfolio with discipline, focusing on high-quality assets and structures to aim to generate attractive risk-adjusted returns for our investors.

The pool of nine assets was acquired as a single portfolio and contributed into the platform’s inaugural ABS, increasing asset and lessee diversification and supporting attractive execution. The efficient financing structure is highly accretive to the Fund with minimal equity exposure and reflects the Aircraft Fund’s opportunistic allocation, which complements the core strategy and supports attractive risk-adjusted returns. • American Airlines: American Airlines is one of the largest global carriers by fleet and network scale, supported by strong liquidity and Tier 1 credit. We view the airline’s scale, operating history, and long-term fleet strategy favorably. • Ethiopian Airlines: Ethiopian Airlines is the flag carrier of Ethiopia and the largest airline in Africa, benefiting from consistent government support and a strong long-term operating track record. Its modern fleet and history of operating aircraft through full useful lives support long-term asset stability. • GOL: GOL is one of the leading low-cost carriers in Latin America with a strong domestic franchise in Brazil and a scaled, single-fleet operating model. Following its recent Chapter 11 exit, the airline has improved its liquidity and balance sheet, positioning it for more stable operations and fleet utilization going forward. • Jetstar Japan: Joint venture between Japan Airlines and Qantas that has returned to improving profitability following the post-COVID recovery. The airline’s strategic role within the Japan Airlines and Qantas networks and parent support underpin its credit and asset quality. • Lion Air: Lion Air is a leading Southeast Asian low-cost carrier with significant scale and a large installed fleet. Ongoing fleet modernization and improving fundamentals support continued utilization of the assets. • Thai Lion Air: Thai Lion Air operates as an ultra-low-cost carrier focused on the domestic Thai market with traffic trends continuing to recover. The airline’s operating model and market positioning support consistent aircraft utilization. Virgin Australia: Virgin Australia is a leading Australian carrier with a strong domestic network and a well-established • brand in core business and leisure routes. Following its recapitalization, the airline has demonstrated improving fundamentals and operating stability, which we believe supports consistent fleet utilization and asset performance. • Vueling: European low-cost carrier owned by IAG, benefiting from investment-grade parent support and strong liquidity. Its narrowbody fleet is highly liquid and well positioned for redeployment across European markets.

blocks.html: PERFORMANCE CALCULATIONS METHODOLOGIES 1. Multiple of Money (MoM) is equal to the total value for each investment divided by the investment amount for such investment. 2. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a measure of the discounted cash flows (inflows and outflows) related to an investment. Specifically, IRR is the discount rate at which the net present value of all cash flows and any remaining investment value is equal to zero. In other words, IRR is the discount rate at which the (i) present value of all capital invested in an investment (including expenses specifically allocable to the investment) is equal to (ii) the present value of all returns from the investment (whether or not realized). 3. Net IRR (To Date) reflects the impact of management fees, fund expenses and carried interest or incentive fee allocations that have been allocated to limited partners. 4. In certain vehicles Bain Capital Special Situations has deferred portions of carried interest accrual to the General Partner as contemplated within the applicable vehicle’s legal documents. During the deferral period, accrued carried interest is not reallocated from the limited partners’ book capital accounts to the account of the General Partner. 5. IRRs shown include all returns generated by reinvested capital and profit. 6. Annualized returns are computed based on the change in value during the period of a theoretical investment made at the beginning of the period. The change in value of a theoretical investment is measured by comparing the aggregate ending value of Limited Partners with the aggregate beginning value adjusted for cash flows related to capital contributions or withdrawals during the period. Returns are geometrically linked on a monthly basis.

blocks.html: The Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 Portfolios are distinct groups of aircrafts owned by the Bain Capital and Griffin Global Asset Management platform. Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are owned by different Bain Capital Special Situations’ Funds though all aircraft across Vintages are held within a corporate entity where any related financing is comingled, i.e. the Bain Capital / Griffin Platform. Further details on the portfolio are noted below. 1. Vintage 1: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on January 7, 2021 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations I and Special Situations Asia I. As of December 31, 2024, the Vintage 1 portfolio owns 34 delivered aircraft. 2. Vintage 2: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on September 23, 2022 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations II and Special Situations Asia II. As of December 31, 2024, the Vintage 2 portfolio owns 31 delivered aircraft and 27 engines. 3. Combined returns for Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are extracted performance across multiple funds and may be deemed to be “hypothetical” performance. Hypothetical performance is subject to inherent limitations, as the performance may have been different had the investments been selected to occur in one fund. 4. Net returns were calculated using the following assumptions and in line with the undiscounted Aircraft Fund fees and expenses reflected in the offering documents: a) Management fees are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 1.50%. b) Carried interest percentage is 20% c) Operating expenses are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 0.25%
